pathways.title: An email account is taken over and the organisation's own invoices are used to divert its income

structure.title: An email account is taken over and the organisation's own invoices are used to divert its income
structure.actor: An outsider who gains access to a staff mailbox through a stolen password.
structure.opportunity: The mailbox has no multi-factor sign-in, so a password is enough to enter it, read correspondence and send from it.
structure.entryPoint: A phishing message or a password reused from another site.
structure.mechanism: The attacker watches correspondence with clients and, at the right moment, sends a genuine-looking invoice or notice with changed bank details from the real account.
structure.controlRelied: Email accounts are not protected by multi-factor sign-in.
structure.concealment: The message comes from the organisation's real address, so clients have no reason to doubt it; the attacker may set rules that hide replies from the mailbox owner.
structure.consequence: Client payments are lost, the organisation may still need to recover its fees, and clients' trust in its correspondence is damaged.
warningIndicators: Clients querying a change of bank details
Unfamiliar sign-ins or forwarding rules on a mailbox
Sent messages the owner did not write
structure.containment: Reset the account and remove any forwarding rules, notify clients through a known channel, and preserve the sign-in and message logs.
structure.longTerm: Every email account is protected by multi-factor sign-in, and clients are told how the organisation will confirm any change of bank details.

pathways.title: A cloned voice of a senior person instructs an urgent payment

structure.title: A cloned voice of a senior person instructs an urgent payment
structure.actor: An outsider using a cloned voice, a voice note or a manipulated video of an executive or owner, built from recordings that are publicly available.
structure.opportunity: Staff act on instructions from senior people, and recognising the voice has always been enough.
structure.entryPoint: A call or voice note, apparently from the chief executive or owner, asking for an urgent and confidential payment.
structure.mechanism: The instruction is urgent and comes from a voice the employee knows, so the payment is made outside the normal process or pushed through it quickly.
structure.controlRelied: There is no agreed method, such as a call-back on a known number or a code word, that verifies a request made by phone, voice note or video, and executives are not bound by it.
structure.concealment: The employee believes the instruction was genuine and the payment appears properly authorised until the executive is asked about it.
structure.consequence: A payment lost to an account that is quickly emptied, with the added harm that staff no longer trust instructions from their own leaders.
warningIndicators: An instruction that insists on secrecy or bypasses the normal process
Urgency with a reason why the executive cannot be called back
A request from an unfamiliar number or account
A new beneficiary on an executive instruction
structure.containment: Call the executive back on a known number, contact the bank to recall the payment, and preserve the call, message and payment records.
structure.longTerm: An agreed verification method applies to every request made by phone, voice note or video, to everyone including executives, and staff are expected to use it.

pathways.title: A payment instruction received by email is acted on without separate confirmation

structure.title: A payment instruction received by email is acted on without separate confirmation
structure.actor: An outsider sending a convincing email that appears to come from the owner, a supplier or a client.
structure.opportunity: Payment, salary and urgent requests received by email are processed on the strength of the email itself.
structure.entryPoint: An email instructing an urgent payment or a change of bank details, often timed for when the sender is known to be unavailable.
structure.mechanism: The request looks routine and comes from a familiar name, so it is processed in the ordinary way.
structure.controlRelied: There is no organisation-wide rule requiring every payment, salary or urgent request received by email to be confirmed through a separate, known channel.
structure.concealment: The payment is properly processed against a request that appears genuine; the fraud is found only when the supposed sender is asked.
structure.consequence: A payment lost to an account that is quickly emptied, and recovery that depends on how quickly the bank is alerted.
warningIndicators: Urgency and a reason why the sender cannot be reached
A new beneficiary or changed bank details
An instruction to keep the request confidential
structure.containment: Contact the bank to recall the payment, confirm with the supposed sender through a known number, and preserve the email and payment records.
structure.longTerm: Every payment, salary or urgent request received by email is confirmed through a separate, known channel before it is acted on.

pathways.title: A help desk reset hands an attacker the account that moves money

structure.title: A help desk reset hands an attacker the account that moves money
structure.actor: An outsider impersonating an employee to the help desk or the IT provider.
structure.opportunity: Password and multi-factor resets are made on the caller's word, and the systems that move money accept the reset account.
structure.entryPoint: A call or message to the help desk asking for a password or multi-factor reset, often claiming a lost phone.
structure.mechanism: The reset is made, the attacker signs in as the employee and uses the employee's access to change bank details or release payments.
structure.controlRelied: Help desk resets are not verified through a route the caller does not control, and systems that move money are not protected by strong sign-in.
structure.concealment: The activity is carried out under a real employee's account, so it looks like ordinary work.
structure.consequence: Payments or changes made under a legitimate account, and the difficulty of proving who acted.
warningIndicators: A reset request claiming a lost phone or urgency
A reset followed quickly by payment or bank-detail activity
Sign-ins from an unusual location or device
An employee unaware of a reset made in their name
structure.containment: Lock the account, reverse the changes, contact the bank about any payment, and preserve the help desk and sign-in records.
structure.longTerm: Every password or multi-factor reset is verified through a route the caller does not control, and systems that move money require strong sign-in.

decisions.question: Name one accountable executive for each area with open or unresolved scenarios: digital channels (10).
decisions.why: Each scenario needs one person with authority over the process, the system and the people involved.
decisions.delay: Open scenarios have no owner, and the controls that stop them stay unassigned.

options.label: One accountable executive per area
options.description: Each area with open scenarios has one executive accountable for its controls, as the method suggests.
options.effort: Low to decide; ongoing for each executive.
options.benefit: Clear ownership that matches how the organisation is run.
options.tradeOff: Requirements that span areas, such as how changes to payment details are verified, need coordination across owners.

options.label: One executive for the whole programme
options.description: A single executive owns every open scenario and directs area leads.
options.benefit: One point of accountability and a consistent approach.
options.tradeOff: Area executives may treat the work as someone else's.

options.label: Area owners with a programme coordinator
options.description: Area executives own their scenarios, and the fraud risk lead coordinates requirements that span areas and reports progress.
options.benefit: Ownership stays in the areas while cross-area requirements are handled once.
options.tradeOff: Needs a coordinator with enough standing to hold owners to account.

options.recommended: Area owners with a programme coordinator.
options.rationale: The open scenarios sit in the operating areas, so ownership belongs there; several of the requirements span areas and are best designed once.

decisions.question: Decide the order in which the open scenarios are addressed, using explicit factors.
decisions.why: MK has not approved a method for rating fraud risks, so this report does not rank them, and neither its order nor the method's tiers is a ranking.
decisions.delay: Effort is spread across every scenario at once, or follows the order of this report, which is not a ranking.

options.label: Explicit factors, settled facts first
options.description: Answers to settle come first; then each open scenario is weighed on how far its control is reported in place, whether money, pay, cash or stock can leave without it, how much of the activity exists, and what management already knows of incidents.
options.benefit: A defensible order that management can explain to the oversight body.
options.tradeOff: Depends on information management must supply, such as volumes and known incidents.

options.label: Area by area
options.description: One area is completed before the next begins.
options.tradeOff: Requirements that span areas are designed several times, and exposure in later areas waits.

options.label: Cross-area requirements first
options.description: Requirements that span areas, such as verifying changes to payment details, are designed once and applied everywhere, before area-specific controls.
options.benefit: One design closes several scenarios at once.
options.tradeOff: Area-specific exposures wait until the shared designs are complete.

options.recommended: Explicit factors, settled facts first, applying cross-area requirements once where they arise.
options.rationale: An order of work should rest on facts management can state and defend to its oversight body, and designing shared requirements once avoids building the same control several times.

decisions.question: Have the owners receive the status of the open and unresolved scenarios at each of its meetings until each is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
decisions.why: Regular reporting keeps the scenarios visible to the people who can remove blockers.
decisions.when: From the first meeting after this report.
decisions.delay: Progress is not visible until the next assessment.

options.label: At each meeting of the oversight body
options.description: A one-page status per open scenario at each meeting until it is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
options.benefit: Keeps the scenarios visible to the people who can remove blockers.
options.tradeOff: Adds to the oversight body's agenda.

options.label: Quarterly summary
options.benefit: Less frequent demand on the oversight body.
options.tradeOff: Blockers may wait a quarter before they are seen.

options.label: Exceptions only
options.description: Only scenarios that are late or blocked are reported.
options.tradeOff: The oversight body does not see progress, and a scenario can drift without being reported as an exception.

options.recommended: At each meeting of the oversight body, until each open scenario is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
options.rationale: Regular reporting is what keeps a programme moving once the first controls are in place.

roadmap.label: Stabilise
roadmap.purpose: Name the owners, decide the order of work and approve the designs.
outcomes: Order of work recorded with its factors

items.text: Name the executive accountable for digital channels, where 10 scenarios are open or unresolved.
items.deliverable: A named accountable executive for the area.

items.text: Decide which of the 10 scenarios with a control reported as a gap to address in this cycle, and in what order, using the decision factors in the finding register.
items.deliverable: A recorded selection and order, with the factors that decided each choice.

items.text: Approve the target design for each selected control, using the target practice, records and measure in the control blueprint register.
items.deliverable: Approved designs, each with an owner and the records it will keep.

scorecard.measure: All staff who act on requests by phone, voice note or video were briefed by the end of the period, and the most recent test found the rule followed in every case tested, including requests that appeared to come from executives.
scorecard.escalation: Any exception not closed by the next review, or any review missed, is reported to the chief financial officer.

scorecard.measure: In the period, the procedure was tested or used, and every compromise discovered was notified as soon as reasonably possible, with any delay justified and recorded.
scorecard.escalation: Any exception not closed by the next review, or any review missed, is reported to the chief financial officer.

scorecard.measure: All staff who act on payment or salary requests were briefed by the end of the period, and the most recent test found the rule followed in every case tested.
scorecard.escalation: Any exception not closed by the next review, or any review missed, is reported to the chief financial officer.

scorecard.measure: At the end of the period, the email security report shows multi-factor authentication on every email account, including executives' and shared mailboxes, and any exception is approved and recorded.
scorecard.escalation: Any exception not closed by the next review, or any review missed, is reported to the chief financial officer.

scorecard.measure: Every password or multi-factor reset made in the period was confirmed through a route the caller did not control before it took effect, or is a recorded and approved exception.
scorecard.escalation: Any case handled without the check, or any exception approved, is reported to the chief financial officer within the month.

scorecard.measure: Open scenarios with a named owner and a recorded decision to address, defer or accept them
scorecard.escalation: A scenario without an owner after 60 days is reported to the oversight body.

scorecard.measure: Priority controls that have met their success measure for a full operating cycle
scorecard.escalation: A control that misses its measure twice is reported with its owner's correction plan.
A missed report is itself reported at the next meeting.

legal.question: Compromises reported as POPIA requires
legal.text: Is there a procedure to notify the Information Regulator, through its eServices portal, and the affected people of a security compromise as soon as reasonably possible after it is discovered, as section 22 of POPIA requires, with any delay justified and recorded?

selectionRules.themes: A theme is reported where the method supports a pattern: answers to settle together with weaker related practices (five or more), outstanding answers (five or more), areas fully in place set against areas mostly open (two or more of each), one area holding most open scenarios, or one of the method's cross-area objectives reported weaker in two or more areas. Up to five, in that order.
selectionRules.findings: Every scenario with answers to settle or a question to clarify, then one scenario from each theme in turn, choosing the one with more core controls reported absent, then more related practices reported weaker, then the method's order; up to 7. This is a selection rule, not a ranking: MK has not approved a prioritisation method.
selectionRules.pathways: Findings with an approved scenario structure, one per theme where possible; up to 4.
selectionRules.priorities: Settling answers comes first where there are any; then the controls that close the selected findings, controls to put in place before practices to strengthen, up to six in all.
selectionRules.blueprints: The controls among the priorities, up to five.

boundary: Every finding rests on the organisation's own answers. MK has not examined documents, interviewed staff or tested any control.
Records named are records management should maintain. MK has not reviewed them.
Independent evidence review and validation belong to MK Advisory, which is scoped and priced separately.
prohibited: Any score, maturity band or readiness level other than the labelled calculated test result
Any statement that a risk is high, critical, the most material or the highest priority
Any claim that a control was tested, verified, validated or confirmed by MK
Any incident, loss, Rand amount, supplier, system or person not in the Fact Pack
Any scenario, finding, control, decision option or owner not in the Fact Pack
